mentions.text: Web services don’t cache private info across users. Consider a file storage service. You might have the client hash the file before uploading and skip the upload if you already have a file with that hash. This is smart design if it’s being used as a sync service. You might make this happen systemwide, so if user A uploads a file and then B uploads the same file, B can skip the upload. This must not be done. Your service now becomes an oracle that tells you whether someone else using the service has uploaded a particular document. Find a document that gets filled out with name and date of birth, and if you know the name of someone using the service and they’ve uploaded a filled-out copy of this document, you can discover their date of birth. Put more concretely, it’s OK if Netflix caches across users (technically, someone can leak the data that someone in the metro area has recently watched Morbius, but the amount of data leaked is too small to matter) but not ok if Gmail does it. A KV cache shared across users is pretty dangerous and I’m surprised anyone does this, aside from some known fixed prefixes.

God knows I've played many thousands of hours of PoE by now. It all comes down to how shitty the implementation is. Everybody used to love Netflix, and pirating movies and shows was essentially dead for a decade. Now the service is shit and pirating is back. It all comes down to the path of least resistance. If that turns out to be getting an LLM to spin up a mock server based only on network emissions from the running program, then that's what will happen. Or if the implementation is so cumbersome that it makes the experience significantly worse, somebody else will build a game not requiring it and take its market share

mentions.text: Speed is the most important thing now. Disaggregated inference is enabling 10x+ speedups on frontier models. It's only going to get faster. When your ultrafast coding agent can do in five minutes what used to take nearly an hour, entire new ways of working are possible. You can solve problems with the business in real time. The need for a software development process begins to evaporate when everything can happen synchronously. Why would the business bother writing a design ticket when they know they could get on a screen share with engineering for roughly 15 minutes and achieve a guaranteed result by the end? They get way more control over the outcome too. Once everyone had broadband internet, Netflix didn't try to mail DVDs faster. They turned into a film studio. Anyone with a software business needs to start thinking along similar lines.

mentions.text: I would think it's more an issue of streaming services, not piracy. There are so many streaming services and every single one wants exclusive content. Rather than the best of the best stories making it through the studio vetting process, streaming services just throw any junk against the wall to see what sticks. Smartphones also play a role. These streaming services know people aren't fully paying attention. They are messing around on their phone while the movie plays, so the movies repeat stuff and make it really obvious, which dumbs down the movie for anyone who is actually fully watching it. Matt Damon confirmed this was something they were told to do in one of his movies that went to Netflix. Looking at the top movies by adjusted gross[0], it was trending up since 2000, peaking from 2016-2019, then it fell off a cliff. There aren't any movies in the top 200 from 2022 or beyond. The pandemic is the obvious reason for the fall off, but that also was a huge boon for the streaming services and poured gasoline on that whole industry, which led to the things mentioned above. Movie piracy has been around for 25 years and the trends in those numbers don't follow along with it. [0] http

mentions.text: Because of nonlinearities in the exponents. Each win compounds faster than compounding of a loss. A near inverse of the Kelly criterion. In mature markets (financial services in 2008) the risk is a zero sum game and there is no super-exponential compounding. In fact the opposite holds true - if you have more AUM your ability to extract proportionally more money from the market diminishes. In the startup world, where you create new markets, Jevons paradox grants you that super-exponential growth. Nvidia, SpaceX and probably a few others.. are the rare ones that are huge, and yet non-saturated market creators. Apple is saturated. So is Meta, Netflix, Alphabet, etc. Microsoft is a wildcard a bit with OpenAI stake, but.. maybe? Amazon is habitually saturated but actually most adapted to it.
